A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GEM, with matching core methods, datasets and experiments. The main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the relocated case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original grounded ECG understanding and ECG-Bench results, modality ablations and qualitative cardiologist assessments.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds PTB-XL grounded understanding results and quantitative cardiologist assessments of GPT-4o, Deepseek-R1 and GEM outputs.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.5 retain the ECG-CoCa and CLIP encoders, projection and concatenation procedure, physiological features, diagnosis guider, training objective and frozen-encoder training. Grounding Feature Extractor renames the existing FeatureDB component. Testing Deepseek-R1 as an alternative data generator does not establish a revised GEM procedure.

E1.justification: The Grounded ECG Understanding task expands from MIMIC-IV-ECG alone to an additional out-of-domain PTB-XL evaluation with 2,041 samples. Although PTB-XL already appeared in ECG-Bench, evaluating detailed grounded interpretations introduces distinct task coverage and external generalization evidence. Existing training datasets and ECG-Bench coverage remain.

E2.justification: Deepseek-R1 enters the clinician-rated comparison of generated training data and GEM outputs in v2 Tables 4–5. PULSE remains the grounded-task comparator, and Random, GPT-4o and PULSE remain the ECG-Bench comparators. The comparator expansion is confined to the new generation-quality evaluation.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 supplements qualitative expert highlighting with a structured assessment of 200 outputs each from GPT-4o, Deepseek-R1 and GEM by eight cardiologists, using seven criteria scored from 1 to 5. Appendix A.2 also changes the stated lead-coverage measure from a count to a percentage and explicitly describes lead accuracy as a percentage. These are reported evaluation changes, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds the PTB-XL distribution-shift evaluation, tests an open-source substitute for instruction generation, and introduces expert-feedback-based failure analysis in Section 4.5. The latter identifies missed waveform abnormalities and overstated severity. The original TS-only/TS+IMG ablations and six case studies in Figures 4–9 are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 4–5 newly report means and standard deviations for cardiologist ratings; v1 has no analogous dispersion reporting. This addition is limited to human assessments. Training-seed variability, confidence intervals and formal significance tests are not introduced; v2's checklist explicitly states that formal significance testing was omitted.

E6.justification: v2 adds PTB-XL grounded results and quantitative clinician ratings, while revising existing MIMIC-IV-ECG results. PULSE and GEM-LLaVA diagnosis accuracy change from 75.94 and 86.34 to 81.14 and 87.24. GEM-LLaVA grounding changes from 74.48 to 75.48, reversing the GEM-backbone ranking on that metric. Lead scores also change, and the former Average entries disappear. ECG-Bench results are unchanged. The revised scores should not be treated as established same-setting gains because their provenance is unexplained and scoring documentation changes.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same mathematical formulations for encoding, alignment, data generation and training. Neither version supplies theoretical results or proofs, and v2 introduces no substantive derivation or formal assumption.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified ECG time-series/image/text model, a 30,000-pair heartbeat-grounded dataset, and the Grounded ECG Understanding task, with improved prediction, explainability and grounding. Additional validation and the updated headline grounding margin do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 newly hypothesizes links between missed abnormalities and representation/data-coverage limitations, and between exaggerated severity and missing patient context. v2 also interprets its new results as supporting out-of-domain reasoning and open-source generation. Appendix A.6 explicitly restricts intended use to research and assistance, extending v1's discussion of GPT-4o disagreements and future improvements.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 changes ECG-Grounding availability from a promised release to a reported completed release, and the abstract explicitly advertises code, model and data access. Appendix A.3 expands evaluation-response examples, while the checklist states that instructions and settings accompany the code. These are documentation and access claims in the PDFs; external availability was not verified.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds discussion of JoLT. References are refreshed with Deepseek-R1, newer vision-language surveys and medical models including MedGemma, UniECG and ECG-LM, while older citations such as MiniGPT-4, Shikra and CardioGPT disappear. The principal positioning around combined ECG modalities and grounded interpretation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify the introduction's modeling and data challenges, rename methodological headings and revise the conclusion. Metric descriptions move from the main text to Appendix A.2, and the appendices gain a contents page and reorganized subsections. The main section sequence and most methodological prose remain stable.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column NeurIPS layout. v1 Tables 1–2 are consolidated into an expanded v2 Table 1, and four new tables present clinician results and scoring rubrics. Figures are resized and architecture labels revised; the six original case-study figures retain their content.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its grounded-understanding task primarily through single-dataset GPT-4o scoring and illustrative expert cases. v2 adds a 2,041-sample external evaluation and a defined eight-cardiologist assessment of 600 outputs, with scoring rubrics and dispersion reporting. These additions substantially strengthen evidence about generalization and interpretation quality, while specific failure analysis clarifies limitations. Unexplained revisions to existing scores and absent formal significance tests remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the added validation.
